L14: # SIPP: Safe Interval Path Planning for Dynamic Environments
L15: ## Authors:
L16: 
L17: Mike Phillips and cite8†Maxim Likhachev†www.ri.cmu.edu L18: 
L19: cite2†Conference Paper L20: 
L21: Proceedings of (ICRA) International Conference on Robotics and Automation

L23: * * *
L24: ## Abstract:
L25: Robotic path planning in static environments is a thoroughly studied problem that can typically be solved very efficiently. However, planning in the presence of dynamic obstacles is still computationally challenging because it requires adding time as an additional dimension to the search-space explored by the planner.
L26: In order to avoid the increase in the dimensionality of the planning problem, most real-time approaches to path planning treat dynamic obstacles as static and constantly re-plan as dynamic obstacles move. Although gaining efficiency, these approaches sacrifice optimality and even completeness.
L27: In this paper, we develop a planner that builds on the observation that while the number of safe timesteps in any configuration may be unbounded, the number of safe time intervals in a configuration is finite and generally very small. A safe interval is a time period for a configuration with no collisions and if it were extended one timestep in either direction, it would then be in collision.
L28: The planner exploits this observation and constructs a search-space with states defined by their configuration and safe interval, resulting in a graph that generally only has a few states per configuration. On the theoretical side, we show that our planner can provide the same optimality and completeness guarantees as planning with time as an additional dimension.
L29: On the experimental side, in simulation tests with up to 200 dynamic obstacles, we show that our planner is significantly faster, making it feasible to use in real-time on robots operating in large dynamic environments. We also ran several real robot trials on the PR2, a mobile manipulation platform.

L22: cite3†Re-use permissions†s100.copyright.com L23: # Motion Planning in Dynamic Environments Using Velocity Obstacles
L24: 
L25: cite4†Paolo Fiorini and cite5†Zvi Shiller cite6†View all authors and affiliations L26: 
L27: cite7†Volume 17, Issue 7 L28: 
L29: cite8†https://doi.org/10.1177/027836499801700706†doi.org L30: ## Abstract
L31: 
L32: This paper presents a method for robot motion planning in dynamic environments. It consists of selecting avoidance maneuvers to avoid static and moving obstacles in the velocity space, based on the cur rent positions and velocities of the robot and obstacles. It is a first- order method, since it does not integrate velocities to yield positions as functions of time.
L33: The avoidance maneuvers are generated by selecting robot ve locities outside of the velocity obstacles, which represent the set of robot velocities that would result in a collision with a given obstacle that moves at a given velocity, at some future time. To ensure that the avoidance maneuver is dynamically feasible, the set of avoidance velocities is intersected with the set of admissible velocities, defined by the robot's acceleration constraints.
L34: Computing new avoidance maneuvers at regular time intervals accounts for general obstacle trajectories.
L35: The trajectory from start to goal is computed by searching a tree of feasible avoidance maneuvers, computed at discrete time intervals. An exhaustive search of the tree yields near-optimal trajectories that either minimize distance or motion time. A heuristic search of the tree is applicable to on-line planning. The method is demonstrated for point and disk robots among static and moving obstacles, and for an automated vehicle in an intelligent vehicle highway system scenario.

L0: # Optimal Reciprocal Collision Avoidance
L1: 
L2: Jur van den Berg, cite0†Stephen J. Guy†www-users.cs.umn.edu , cite1†Jamie Snape†wwwx.cs.unc.edu , cite2†Ming C. Lin†www.cs.unc.edu , and cite3†Dinesh Manocha†www.cs.unc.edu L3: Department of Computer Science, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
L4: ## Description
L5: We present a formal approach to reciprocal collision avoidance, where multiple independent mobile robots or agents need to avoid collisions with each other without communication among agents while moving in a common workspace. Our formulation, optimal reciprocal collision avoidance (ORCA), provides sufficient conditions for collision-free motion by letting each agent take half of the responsibility of avoiding pairwise collisions.
L6: Selecting the optimal action for each agent is reduced to solving a low-dimensional linear program, and we prove that the resulting motions are smooth. We test our optimal reciprocal collision avoidance approach on a team of cite4†iRobot Create†www.irobot.com differential-drive mobile robots, as well as on several dense and complex simulation scenarios in both 2D and 3D workspaces involving thousands of agents, and compute collision-free actions for all of them in only a few milliseconds.

L3@P0: Abstract— Robotic path planning in static environments is
L4@P0: a thoroughly studied problem that can typically be solved
L5@P0: very efficiently. However, planning in the presence of dynamic
L6@P0: obstacles is still computationally challenging because it requires
L7@P0: adding time as an additional dimension to the search-space
L23@P0: theoretical side, we show that our planner can provide the
L24@P0: same optimality and completeness guarantees as planning with
L25@P0: time as an additional dimension. On the experimental side, in
L26@P0: simulation tests with up to 200 dynamic obstacles, we show that
L27@P0: our planner is significantly faster, making it feasible to use in
L28@P0: real-time on robots operating in large dynamic environments.

L31@P0: I. INTRODUCTION
L32@P0: Whether it be autonomously driving a vehicle or performing household jobs, such as cleaning a room, almost all tasks
L33@P0: that robots perform assume the ability to safely navigate from
L34@P0: place to place in the presence of moving objects such as
L35@P0: people, pets, cars, etc. In order to accomplish this, robots
L36@P0: need to be able to predict where these dynamic obstacles will
L37@P0: be moving in the near future. They need to plan short paths
L38@P0: to their goals that do not endanger or inconvenience people.
L39@P0: Robots also need to be able to plan these paths very quickly,
L40@P0: in the likely situation that a dynamic obstacle’s trajectory is
L41@P0: not what the robot predicted, and a new plan must be created
L42@P0: to prevent collision. Being able to plan paths efficiently will
L43@P0: allow robots to be more responsive and robust to a constantly
L44@P0: changing environment.
L45@P0: When planning in dynamic environments, adding a time
L46@P0: dimension to the state-space is needed in order to properly
L47@P0: handle moving obstacles, shown in Figure 1(b). However, the
L48@P0: large increase in the number of states to be searched causes
L49@P0: planning times to be much longer. Since the environment
L50@P0: is constantly changing, plans need to be generated quickly
L51@P0: or they will be out of date before they can even be used.

L69@P0: Therefore, for practical purposes, a common approach to
L70@P0: producing faster plans is to treat the environment as though
L71@P0: it were static [5], [9]. This is done by turning each dynamic
L72@P0: obstacle (and sometimes its predicted trajectory for the near
L73@P0: future) into a static obstacle. This ensures that the plan
L74@P0: generated will not be allowed to collide with the dynamic
L75@P0: obstacle in the near future. However, this approach suffers
L76@P0: from suboptimality in cases where the robot could have
L77@P0: crossed a trajectory without being hit, or just waited until
L78@P0: the obstacle passed and then crossed. Instead it takes a long
L79@P0: path around the trajectory of the obstacle. There are even
L80@P0: cases when this approach will fail to find a solution at all,
L81@P0: such as when a dynamic obstacle’s trajectory goes through
L82@P0: or crosses in front of a doorway that the robot must also use
L83@P0: in order to reach its goal, shown in Figure 1(a).
L84@P0: In this paper we propose a method that exploits the
L85@P0: observation that the number of contiguous safe intervals is
L86@P0: generally significantly smaller than the number of timesteps
L87@P0: that compose those intervals. For example, a configuration
L88@P0: that no dynamic obstacles pass through only has one safe
L89@P0-1: interval, which spans from the start time to infinity. Withthis in mind, we develop a planner that uses states defined by
L90@P1: configuration (x,y,θ,etc) and the safe interval as independent
L91@P1: variables, while only storing the actual timestep as a dependent variable. A configuration is the set of non-time variables
L92@P1: that describe the robot’s state, such as position, heading, joint
L93@P1: angles, etc. An independent variable is one that is used to
L94@P1: actually identify a state, while a dependent variable is stored
L95@P1: with the state but is not used to identify it. Specifically, two
L96@P1: states with the same values for their independent variables,
L97@P1: but different dependent ones, are still considered the same
L98@P1: state, by the planner. We provide theoretical guarantees that
L99@P1: the states we eliminate from consideration cannot be part
L100@P1: of the optimal solution with respect to the time it takes
L101@P1: to traverse the path. As a result, our planner can guarantee
L102@P1: optimality, while avoiding the increase in dimensionality of
L103@P1: the problem. We demonstrate the efficiency in simulation
L104@P1: with experiments on randomly generated indoor and outdoor
L105@P1: environments, showing a significant speed increase over a
L106@P1: planner that represents states with configuration and timestep
L107@P1: as independent variables. Using the PR2 robot, we also
L108@P1: demonstrate that the planner is suitable for real-time use.
L109@P1: II. RELATED WORK
L110@P1: Most of the approaches to dealing with dynamic obstacles,
L111@P1: model them as static obstacles with a short window of high
L112@P1: cost around the beginning of their projected trajectories [5],
L113@P1: [9]. While efficient, these approaches suffer from potential
L114@P1: high suboptimality and even incompleteness, as described
L115@P1: in our introduction. Another common approach is to only
L116@P1: consider dynamic obstacles (still treating them as static
L117@P1: obstacles) while executing the path, using local obstacle
L118@P1: avoidance methods [2]. This method can get stuck in local
L119@P1: minima and is not globally optimal. Another alternative is for
L120@P1: the local planner to use velocity obstacles, which determine
L121@P1: the controls that lead to collision with moving obstacles [13].
L122@P1: While this is more accurate, it still can lead to local minima
L123@P1: as it greedily minimizes the difference between the desired
L124@P1: control without dynamic obstacles, and the set of feasible
L125@P1: controls that are not in velocity obstacles.
L126@P1: Some approaches plan in the full space-time search space
L127@P1: [10]. Silver’s HCA* algorithm is designed for planning
L128@P1: for multiple robots, but in the paper, he points out that it
L129@P1: can be applied to planning in dynamic environments. In
L138@P1: also large. Our algorithm groups contiguous, collision-free
L139@P1: timesteps into safe intervals, and then represents each state by
L140@P1: a (configuration, safe interval) pair. The maximum number
L141@P1: of safe intervals for any given configuration is at most the
L142@P1: number of dynamic obstacles whose trajectories intersect in
L143@P1: that configuration. Therefore, the number of safe intervals
L144@P1: is significantly smaller than the number of timesteps for the
L145@P1: same configuration. As a result, the search space our planner
L146@P1: constructs is much smaller, leading to faster planning and
L147@P1: smaller memory requirements.
L148@P1: The approach [12] is similar to ours in that it recognizes
L149@P1: that a state is only needed for the earliest arrival time in a
L150@P1: safe interval. The major difference is how we evaluate an
L151@P1: edge from one interval to another. In [12], an “expand”
L152@P1: is a partial move of a “probe” along an edge via a single
L153@P1: timestep which then must be replaced back into the queue.
L154@P1: This means that for each edge a “probe” goes back into the
L155@P1: queue many times (and queue operations are the expensive
L156@P1: part of the A* search) instead of just once as it is for our
L157@P1: planner. Essentially, the approach in [12], has taken each
L158@P1: cost-n edge and converted it into n cost-1 edges, which raises
L159@P1: the asymptotic runtime to be a function of the edge weights
L160@P1: as well as the number of vertices and edges. Nevertheless,
L161@P1: [12] is very closely related to our approach.
L162@P1: Planning with time, required for dealing with dynamic
L163@P1: obstacles, is hard to perform on-line, since constant demand
L164@P1: for re-planning enforces tight constraints on execution cycle.
L165@P1: To address the real-time constraints, a number of approaches
L166@P1: have been proposed that sacrifice near-optimality guarantees
L167@P1: for the sake of efficiency [3], [11]. Our proposed approach
L168@P1: differs in that we aim for computing paths that are optimal
L169@P1: with respect to shortest time. Some other approaches use
L170@P1: RRT-variants to plan quickly in higher-dimensional search
L171@P1: spaces that can handle the kinodynamic constraints of more
L172@P1: complex robots [7], [1]. However, these sampling-based
L173@P1: approaches cannot provide the guarantees on optimality that
L174@P1: we strive for. There have also been approaches that plan with
L175@P1: the added time dimension only until the end of an obstacle’s
L176@P1: trajectory (or when the uncertainty about the obstacle is
L177@P1: too large) and then finish the plan in the simpler static
L178@P1: state-space [4]. In this Time-Bounded Lattice approach, the
L179@P1: dynamic obstacles and the time dimension are dropped in the
L180@P1: search space, after a certain point in the time dimension. This
L181@P1: sacrifices optimality. Our algorithm does not prune dynamic
L182@P1: obstacle trajectories at all, making it optimal with respect to
L183@P1: the entire given trajectories.
L184@P1: III. ALGORITHM
L185@P1: We define a safe interval as a contiguous period of time
L186@P1: for a configuration, during which there is no collision and
L187@P1: it is in collision one timestep prior and one timestep after
L188@P1: the period. The obvious exception to this is that the last
L189@P1: safe interval for a configuration may go until infinity, if a
L190@P1: dynamic obstacle never again is predicted to pass through
L191@P1: this configuration. A collision interval is the opposite of a
L192@P1: safe interval. A collision interval is a contiguous period of
L193@P1: time for a configuration, where each timestep in this period
L194@P1: is in collision with a dynamic obstacle and it is safe one
L195@P1: timestep prior and one timestep after the period. Each spatial
L196@P1: configuration (such as the one shown in Figure 2) has a
L197@P1: timeline (Figure 3), which is just an ordered list of intervals,
L198@P1: alternating between safe and collision. Clearly, there cannot
